description: Jay Gatsby throws lavish parties to win Daisy back. Fitzgerald paints the Jazz Age and the corruption of the American dream.

hero.hook: A green light at the end of a dock: the symbol of a past that cannot be bought back.

blocks.text: Published in **1925**, **The Great Gatsby** is the masterpiece of **F. Scott Fitzgerald**, born in **1896** and dead in **1940**. Through **Jay Gatsby**, a mysterious man with fabulous parties, he explores social climbing, the illusion of happiness, and the impossibility of buying back the past.

The novel is a requiem for [[the American Dream]]. That idea holds that in the United States anyone can succeed on merit and hard work alone. Behind the gilding of the Jazz Age, Fitzgerald shows a deep moral rot. Money buys the show, but not redemption.

Fitzgerald lived through the **Roaring Twenties**, the decade the French call the *années folles*. It was a burst of euphoria after the First World War. With his wife **Zelda**, he embodied the glamour and the excess of that lost generation, and also its psychological and financial fragility.

blocks.caption: F. Scott Fitzgerald, chronicler and player of the Roaring Twenties

blocks.text: The novel is set during [[Prohibition]], from **1920** to **1933**. Alcohol was banned by the Constitution. The ban did far more for smuggling and illegal fortunes than for sobriety. Gatsby owes his own wealth to that underground economy. The book sold badly when it came out. Fitzgerald died in **1940** believing he had failed.

blocks.caption: America in the 1920s: parties, jazz, and the illusion of prosperity

blocks.text: The Great Gatsby sold only about 20,000 copies when it was published. It became a classic after Fitzgerald's death, once copies were handed out to soldiers during the Second World War.

sections.title: Fitzgerald and the double edge of the Roaring Twenties

blocks.text: **Jay Gatsby**, born **James Gatz**, the son of poor Dakota farmers, rejects his origins to reinvent himself. His fortune, built on bootlegging during Prohibition, serves one obsession: winning back **Daisy Buchanan**, the woman he loved before the war.

blocks.caption: West Egg and East Egg: Gatsby's mansion looking across at Daisy's

blocks.text: Settled in **West Egg**, the district of the “new money,” Gatsby stares every night at the **green light** at the end of the Buchanans' dock in **East Egg**. East Egg is home to the inherited aristocracy. The light stands for the future he chases and never reaches. Gatsby believes that will alone can erase time, but the past holds.

sections.title: Gatsby, or the invention of the self

blocks.text: The narrator **Nick Carraway**, Daisy's cousin and Gatsby's neighbor, watches this world with fascination and disgust. He sees a nobility in Gatsby despite his crimes, set against the cruelty of the Buchanans, inherited wealth protected by money and indifference.

blocks.attribution: F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby
blocks.text: Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgastic future that year by year recedes before us.

When Daisy kills **Myrtle Wilson** by accident at the wheel of Gatsby's car, she lets him take the blame. Gatsby dies, shot by Myrtle's husband. Nobody comes to his funeral. Nick sees that the whole thing was a mirage: the lavish parties hid an absolute loneliness.

sections.title: Nick Carraway and the eye of the witness

blocks.text: The novel closes on the image of boats beating against the current: our hopes push us forward while the past holds us in place. Fitzgerald also paints the **Valley of Ashes**, a ruined industrial strip. The eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg on a billboard stand for a [[Hidden God]]. Spirituality has given way to commerce.

Rediscovered after **1945**, the book became a mirror of American contradictions: new money against old blood, dream against reality, spectacle against truth. It remains one of the most famous critiques of [[the American Dream]] and of its broken promises.
**The Great Gatsby** traces the tragic fall of a man who tried to buy back his past, and indicts the recklessness of an elite that money keeps safe.

sections.title: Memory, legacy, and the fading of the dream
